Example: 
                    Differentiating a Product
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the function $y = x^5 (\cos x)^x.$ Its derivative is given by

$$
y'(x) = x^4 (\cos x)^x \left( 5 + g(x) \right).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We have the function 

$$
y = x^5 (\cos x)^x.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{5})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{5}{x}+(x)^{′}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+x\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{5}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+x\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{5}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{5}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y = x^5 (\cos x)^x {:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}(\frac{5}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & ={x}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}(\frac{5}{x}+\frac{x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{x}-\frac{{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}(5+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
g(x) = x \ln ( \cos  x ) - x^2 \tan x.
$$

Example: 
                    Differentiating a Quotient
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the function $y = \dfrac{(x+3)^3}{(x+5)^6}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
y' = -\dfrac{g(x)(x+3)^2}{(x+5)^7}.
$$

Find the function $g(x).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We have the function 

$$
y =  \dfrac{(x+3)^3}{(x+5)^6}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{(x+3)^{3}}{(x+5)^{6}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((x+3)^{3})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((x+5)^{6}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+3)-6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+5)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+3)-6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+5)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =3\cdot \frac{1}{x+3}-6\cdot \frac{1}{x+5} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{3}{x+3}-\frac{6}{x+5}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{3}{x+3}-\frac{6}{x+5})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y =  \dfrac{(x+3)^3}{(x+5)^6}{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{(x+3)^{3}}{(x+5)^{6}}(\frac{3}{x+3}-\frac{6}{x+5}) \\  & =\frac{(x+3)^{3}}{(x+5)^{6}}(\frac{3(x+5)-6(x+3)}{(x+3)(x+5)}) \\  & =\frac{(x+3)^{3}}{(x+5)^{6}}(\frac{-3x-3}{(x+3)(x+5)}) \\  & =-\frac{3(x+1)(x+3)^{2}}{(x+5)^{7}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x) = \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{3(x+1)}.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Differentiating a Radical Expression
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the function $y = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{x^2}{x^5+ 1}}.$  The derivative of this function is given by

$$
y' =  \dfrac{g(x)}{3\sqrt[3]{x(x^5+1)^4}}.
$$

Find the function $g(x).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{5}+1}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}}{\sqrt[3]{{x}^{5}+1}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2/3}}{({x}^{5}+1)^{1/3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2/3}}{({x}^{5}+1)^{1/3}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2/3})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{5}+1)^{1/3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{5}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{5}+1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{5}+1}\cdot (5{x}^{4}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{2}{x}-\frac{5{x}^{4}}{{x}^{5}+1})\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{1}{3}(\frac{2}{x}-\frac{5{x}^{4}}{{x}^{5}+1}))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y =  \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{x^2}{x^5+ 1}}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{5}+1}}(\frac{2}{x}-\frac{5{x}^{4}}{{x}^{5}+1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{5}+1}}(\frac{2({x}^{5}+1)-5{x}^{5}}{x({x}^{5}+1)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{5}+1}}(\frac{-3{x}^{5}+2}{x({x}^{5}+1)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{5}+1}}(\frac{-3{x}^{5}+2}{\sqrt[3]{{x}^{3}({x}^{5}+1)^{3}}}) \\  & =\frac{-3{x}^{5}+2}{3\sqrt[3]{x({x}^{5}+1)^{4}}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x) = \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{-3x^5+2}.
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
When a function $y=y(x)$ contains complex products, quotients, or radicals, we can use logarithmic differentiation to find the derivative $y'(x).$ 

For example, consider the following function: 

$$
y = x^2 \cdot 2^x
$$

 

Our goal is to find $y'(x).$ To do this, we will use the product rule for logarithms, namely

$$
\ln(a b)= \ln a + \ln b.
$$

 

We differentiate our function by following four steps.

**Step 1.** We take the natural logarithm of both sides and apply the product and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** Next, we differentiate both sides of our equation using implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{′}+(x)^{′}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot \frac{1}{x}+1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Then, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4.** Finally, we substitute back our original expression for $y =x^2\cdot 2^x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}(\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =x\cdot {2}^{x+1}+{x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Using Logarithms to Differentiate a Quotient
tutorials.problem:
In cases where we wish to differentiate a quotient of functions

$$
y =  f(x) = \dfrac{g(x)}{h(x)},
$$

we can apply the quotient rule for logarithms: 

$$
\ln \left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right) = \ln a - \ln b
$$

 

For example, let's compute $y',$ where the function $y$ is given by

$$
y = \dfrac {e^{x^2}}{(1-2x)^2(x-1)^3}.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{2}(x-1)^{3}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{{x}^{2}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-2x)^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((x-1)^{3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-2x)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-2x)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x-2\cdot \frac{1}{1-2x}\cdot (-2)-3\cdot \frac{1}{x-1} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x+\frac{4}{1-2x}-\frac{3}{x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(2x+\frac{4}{1-2x}-\frac{3}{x-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute our expression for $y,$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{2}(x-1)^{3}}(2x+\frac{4}{1-2x}-\frac{3}{x-1}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{2}(x-1)^{3}}(\frac{2x(1-2x)(x-1)+4(x-1)-3(1-2x)}{(1-2x)(x-1)}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}(2x(1-2x)(x-1)+4(x-1)-3(1-2x)) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}(-4{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}+8x-7) \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}(4{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}-8x+7) \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}(4{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}-8x+7)}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$
